title: Host Software
summary: One of the very first Network Working Group notes, dated April 1969. It sketches how the ARPANET's message processors (IMPs) work and what software the connected host computers would need in order to talk to one another. It also lists open questions and proposes some early experiments. It is a discussion paper, not a specification.

eli5.summary: Before the first computers could chat, someone had to write down what each one would need to do. This note is like a first sketch of the rules for passing notes between classrooms.

subtitle: A 1969 discussion paper on what software the first ARPANET hosts would need to talk to each other.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET's message processors (IMPs) were specified by BB&N, but the host computers attached to them still needed agreed software to talk to each other.
tldr.mechanism: The note summarizes how IMP messages, links and packets work, then sketches host primitives for TTY-like and file-like connections over a reserved control link, plus an idea for running console logic locally.
tldr.outcome: It is explicitly tentative: very little of it is firm, reactions are expected, and it ends with open questions and two proposed experiments.

facts.label: Links per host pair
facts.value: 32, with link 0 reserved for host operating systems

today: RFC 1 is listed as Informational and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes tentative 1969 ideas for the ARPANET, and the text itself says very little of it was firm.

sections.title: Who Wrote What, and Why
sections.content:
The software for the ARPA Network lives partly in the IMPs (the message processors) and partly in the HOSTs (the connected computers). BB&N specified the IMP software. It was left to the HOST groups to agree on the HOST software.

The author, Steve Crocker of UCLA, describes meetings among the initial four sites in the summer of 1968 and a working group of three that met through the fall and winter. He presents tentative agreements and open questions, and says that very little of what is in the note is firm.
sections.eli5: The people who built the network boxes had their part done. The people with the computers still had to agree on how their own part would work, so this note is a first draft of that talk.

sections.title: How the IMPs Move Messages
sections.content:
Hosts exchange information in messages of at most 8080 bits, plus a 16-bit header. The header holds a 5-bit destination, an 8-bit link, a 1-bit trace flag and 2 spare bits. The trace bit tells the IMPs to record status information and send it to the Network Measurement Center at UCLA.

Between every pair of hosts there are 32 logical full-duplex links. A host may not send two successive messages on the same link until the destination IMP returns a special message called an RFNM (Request for Next Message). This limits the congestion one host can cause another, though the text notes it only works if the overload comes from one or two links.

Links are always functioning and there are always 32 of them, so each IMP keeps 18 tables of 32 entries whatever the traffic. The note admits objections but calls the scheme simple and probably better than more complex ones.

Inside the network, an IMP splits a message into packets of at most 1010 bits. A 24-bit cyclic checksum is added by the transmission hardware and checked on receipt, and packets are reassembled into messages at the destination IMP. The note ends this part with four open questions, such as why only 32 links exist when the link field is 8 bits.
sections.eli5: Big notes are cut into small pieces, each with a check number, and put back together at the other end. Each pair of computers gets 32 lanes, and you must wait for a thumbs-up before sending the next note on the same lane.

sections.title: What Hosts Need From Each Other
sections.content:
The note wants the network to be easy to use from day one, so it proposes that any remote host can be used as if it had been dialed up from a teletype (TTY) terminal. It would also like some way to send a file that does not simply imitate a teletype.

A key worry is delay. Every response from a remote host takes on the order of a half-second, which hurts echo-style interaction and is worse for graphics stations or other sophisticated terminals.

The note also asks for host-to-host error checking. Jeff Rulifson of SRI points out that checking at major software interfaces saves dispute and wasted effort. BB&N says the host-IMP hardware will be as reliable as a host's internal registers, but the authors want the check anyway.
sections.eli5: Everyone wants to be able to use a faraway computer as if they were sitting next to it. But every answer takes about half a second, and a double-check on every note would catch mistakes early.

sections.title: Connections, Primitives and Local Consoles
sections.content:
Link 0 is reserved for communication between host operating systems, leaving 31 links to act as dial-up lines. To connect, an operating system picks a free link and sends a request to the remote host over link 0. The remote host agrees by sending an accepting message back over link 0. If both sides choose the same link at the same time, the host with the lower priority gives way, for example by ranking host identification numbers. The result is a TTY-like connection in the pre-log-in state.

For large transfers, user programs at both ends can ask for a second, file-like connection alongside the TTY-like one. It does no searching for interrupt characters and uses buffering suited to higher data rates. The note lists six primitives hosts should offer: initiate, terminate and send or receive for each of the two kinds of connection. For error checking it proposes that each message carry a message number, a bit count and a checksum, with a 16-bit end-around-carry sum computed on 1152 bits and then circularly shifted right one bit.

To avoid half-second delays on trivial keystrokes, it proposes a language for console control, currently named DEL. The remote host would send the DEL source of its console front end, which the local host compiles, so typing like H E L L O with rubouts is handled locally and only H E L P <CR> is sent. Two initial experiments are listed, built around SRI's on-line retrieval system (NLS), with DEL compilers written at all sites.
sections.eli5: Computers use lane 0 to ask each other to open a new lane. And instead of mailing every single keystroke, your computer could run a little helper program that tidies up your typing first and sends only the finished line.
